canonical_cases.case_name: Briggs v. Eden Council for Hope & Opportunity
canonical_cases.court: Supreme Court of California
canonical_cases.holding: California's anti-SLAPP statute applies to all causes of action arising from acts in furtherance of constitutionally protected speech or petitioning, regardless of whether the plaintiff is a public figure or the speech is a matter of public interest.

canonical_cases.case_name: Equilon Enterprises v. Consumer Cause, Inc.
canonical_cases.court: Supreme Court of California
canonical_cases.holding: Defendant invoking § 425.16 need only show the suit arises from protected activity; intent to chill speech is not a separate element.

canonical_statutes.title: California anti-SLAPP - special motion to strike
canonical_statutes.text: (b)(1) A cause of action against a person arising from any act of that person in furtherance of the person's right of petition or free speech under the United States Constitution or the California Constitution in connection with a public issue shall be subject to a special motion to strike, unless the court determines that the plaintiff has established that there is a probability that the plaintiff will prevail on the claim. (e) As used in this section, 'act in furtherance of a person's right of petition or free speech under the United States or California Constitution in connection with a public issue' includes: (1) any written or oral statement or writing made before a legislative, executive, or judicial proceeding; (2) any written or oral statement or writing made in connection with an issue under consideration or review by a legislative, executive, or judicial body; (3) any written or oral statement or writing made in a place open to the public or a public forum in connection with an issue of public interest; (4) any other conduct in furtherance of the exercise of the constitutional right of petition or the constitutional right of free speech in connection with a public issue or an issue of public interest.

canonical_statutes.title: Texas Citizens Participation Act - dismissal procedure
canonical_statutes.text: (27.003)(a) If a legal action is based on or is in response to a party's exercise of the right of free speech, right to petition, or right of association, that party may file a motion to dismiss the legal action. (27.005)(b) The court shall dismiss a legal action against the moving party if the moving party demonstrates that the legal action is based on or is in response to the party's exercise of: (1) the right of free speech; (2) the right to petition; or (3) the right of association. (c) The court may not dismiss a legal action under this section if the party bringing the legal action establishes by clear and specific evidence a prima facie case for each essential element of the claim in question.

doctrines.doctrine_name: BIPA and CUBI - biometric privacy state statutes
doctrines.description: Illinois's Biometric Information Privacy Act creates a private right of action and statutory damages of $1,000 / $5,000 per violation; Texas's CUBI provides only state AG enforcement. The statutes differ sharply on damages, accrual, and consent mechanics.

canonical_cases.case_name: Rosenbach v. Six Flags Entertainment Corp.
canonical_cases.court: Supreme Court of Illinois
canonical_cases.holding: A BIPA plaintiff need not allege an actual injury beyond the statutory violation of the right to control biometric data; technical violations alone confer standing to sue under § 20.

canonical_cases.case_name: Cothron v. White Castle System, Inc.
canonical_cases.court: Supreme Court of Illinois
canonical_cases.holding: Separate claims accrue under BIPA each time a private entity scans or transmits biometric identifiers without complying with §§ 15(b) and 15(d) - opening employers to potentially massive aggregate damages.

canonical_statutes.title: Illinois BIPA - duties and prohibitions
canonical_statutes.text: A private entity may not collect, capture, purchase, receive, or otherwise obtain a person's biometric identifier unless it first: (1) informs the subject in writing that biometric data is being collected and stored; (2) informs the subject of the specific purpose and length of term for collection and storage; and (3) receives a written release. Statutory damages: $1,000 per negligent violation, $5,000 per intentional or reckless violation, plus attorney fees.

canonical_statutes.title: Illinois BIPA - private right of action and damages
canonical_statutes.text: Any person aggrieved by a violation of this Act shall have a right of action in a State circuit court or as a supplemental claim in federal district court against an offending party. A prevailing party may recover for each violation: (1) against a private entity that negligently violates a provision of this Act, liquidated damages of $1,000 or actual damages, whichever is greater; (2) against a private entity that intentionally or recklessly violates a provision of this Act, liquidated damages of $5,000 or actual damages, whichever is greater; (3) reasonable attorneys' fees and costs, including expert witness fees and other litigation expenses; and (4) other relief, including an injunction, as the State or federal court may deem appropriate.

canonical_statutes.title: Texas Capture or Use of Biometric Identifier Act
canonical_statutes.text: (a) In this section, 'biometric identifier' means a retina or iris scan, fingerprint, voiceprint, or record of hand or face geometry. (b) A person may not capture a biometric identifier of an individual for a commercial purpose unless the person: (1) informs the individual before capturing the biometric identifier; and (2) receives the individual's consent to capture the biometric identifier. (d) A person who possesses a biometric identifier of an individual that is captured for a commercial purpose: (1) may not sell, lease, or otherwise disclose the biometric identifier to another person unless permitted by an enumerated exception. Enforcement is by the Attorney General; civil penalty up to $25,000 per violation.

doctrines.doctrine_name: Caremark / Marchand - director oversight liability under Delaware law
doctrines.description: Directors of Delaware corporations face oversight liability under In re Caremark / Marchand when they utterly fail to implement reporting systems or consciously disregard known risks - particularly 'mission critical' regulatory risks.

canonical_cases.case_name: In re Caremark International Inc. Derivative Litigation
canonical_cases.court: Court of Chancery of Delaware
canonical_cases.holding: Directors may be liable for failing to ensure that an information and reporting system exists and provides timely, accurate information for compliance and risk monitoring. Caremark liability requires showing utterly failed oversight or conscious disregard.

canonical_cases.court: Supreme Court of Delaware
canonical_cases.holding: Caremark oversight failures sound in good faith - a director acts in bad faith only by knowing failure to discharge the duty to monitor; held that good-faith reliance on the auditor and internal compliance systems insulated the directors there.

canonical_cases.court: Supreme Court of Delaware
canonical_cases.holding: Where food safety was 'mission critical' to an ice cream company, the board's failure to establish any board-level system for monitoring food safety stated a Caremark claim.

doctrines.doctrine_name: GE Energy v. Outokumpu - non-signatory equitable estoppel under the FAA
doctrines.description: The Federal Arbitration Act does not preempt state-law equitable-estoppel doctrines that permit non-signatories to compel arbitration; international cases under the New York Convention are not excluded.

canonical_cases.case_name: GE Energy Power Conversion France SAS, Corp. v. Outokumpu Stainless USA, LLC
canonical_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
canonical_cases.holding: The New York Convention does not conflict with state-law doctrines of equitable estoppel that allow a non-signatory to compel arbitration of disputes 'arising out of' an agreement with an arbitration clause.

doctrines.doctrine_name: Dutra Group v. Batterton - punitive damages unavailable for unseaworthiness
doctrines.description: Punitive damages are not available for a Jones Act seaman's general-maritime unseaworthiness claim against a vessel owner.

canonical_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
canonical_cases.holding: Punitive damages are unavailable for an unseaworthiness claim under general maritime law; the Court declined to expand the remedies recognized in Atlantic Sounding (which permitted punitive damages for willful denial of maintenance and cure).

canonical_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
canonical_cases.holding: Punitive damages remain available under general maritime law for the willful and wanton failure to provide maintenance and cure to a seaman.

doctrines.doctrine_name: ITC § 337 - patent enforcement and exclusion orders
doctrines.description: Section 337 of the Tariff Act of 1930 (19 U.S.C. § 1337) authorizes the International Trade Commission to investigate and bar imports that infringe U.S. patents, copyrights, trademarks, or trade secrets; the ITC's in rem exclusion orders are independent of district-court remedies.

canonical_cases.case_name: Suprema, Inc. v. International Trade Commission
canonical_cases.court: Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit
canonical_cases.holding: En banc Federal Circuit held that the ITC may bar imports under § 337 based on induced infringement of method claims even if direct infringement occurs only after importation.

canonical_cases.case_name: Spansion, Inc. v. International Trade Commission
canonical_cases.court: Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit
canonical_cases.holding: Once a § 337 violation is established, exclusion orders issue as a matter of course; the public-interest factors limiting exclusion are rarely dispositive.

canonical_statutes.title: Tariff Act § 337 - unfair practices in import trade
canonical_statutes.text: (a)(1) The following are declared unlawful, and when found by the Commission to exist shall be dealt with, in addition to any other provision of law, as provided in this section: (B) The importation into the United States, the sale for importation, or the sale within the United States after importation of articles that (i) infringe a valid and enforceable United States patent or a valid and enforceable United States copyright registered under title 17 ...

doctrines.doctrine_name: EEOC filing deadline (300/180 days) - National R.R. v. Morgan continuing violations
doctrines.description: Discrete discriminatory or retaliatory acts under Title VII must be filed with the EEOC within 300 days (in deferral states) or 180 days; hostile-work-environment claims accrue under the continuing-violations doctrine.

canonical_cases.case_name: National Railroad Passenger Corp. v. Morgan
canonical_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
canonical_cases.holding: Discrete acts (termination, failure to promote, denial of transfer) are independent unlawful employment practices each of which must be timely charged. Hostile-work-environment claims may include conduct outside the limitations window if at least one act contributing to the claim falls within the window.

canonical_statutes.title: Title VII - EEOC filing deadline
canonical_statutes.text: A charge under this section shall be filed within one hundred and eighty days after the alleged unlawful employment practice occurred ... except that in a case of an unlawful employment practice with respect to which the person aggrieved has initially instituted proceedings with a State or local agency with authority to grant or seek relief from such practice ... such charge shall be filed by or on behalf of the person aggrieved within three hundred days after the alleged unlawful employment practice occurred.

doctrines.description: Rule 702 as amended effective December 1, 2023 makes explicit that the proponent must establish admissibility by a preponderance of the evidence and that the expert's opinion must reflect a reliable application of methods to facts. The amendment confirms (but does not change) the gatekeeping function under Daubert / Kumho Tire.

canonical_cases.case_name: Daubert v. Merrell Dow Pharmaceuticals, Inc.
canonical_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
canonical_cases.holding: Federal Rule of Evidence 702 displaced the Frye 'general acceptance' test; judges serve as gatekeepers to ensure expert testimony rests on a reliable foundation and is relevant to the task.

canonical_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
canonical_cases.holding: Daubert's gatekeeping obligation applies to ALL expert testimony, not just scientific testimony; the trial court has broad latitude in deciding how to assess reliability of technical and other specialized expertise.

canonical_statutes.title: Testimony by expert witnesses (post-2023)
canonical_statutes.text: A witness who is qualified as an expert by knowledge, skill, experience, training, or education may testify in the form of an opinion or otherwise if the proponent demonstrates to the court that it is more likely than not that: (a) the expert's scientific, technical, or other specialized knowledge will help the trier of fact to understand the evidence or to determine a fact in issue; (b) the testimony is based on sufficient facts or data; (c) the testimony is the product of reliable principles and methods; and (d) the expert's opinion reflects a reliable application of the principles and methods to the facts of the case.

doctrines.description: After Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard (2023), race-based admissions programs face strict scrutiny that the prior Grutter framework no longer survives; most race-conscious admissions are unconstitutional.

canonical_cases.case_name: Students for Fair Admissions, Inc. v. President & Fellows of Harvard College
canonical_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
canonical_cases.holding: Race-based admissions programs at Harvard and UNC violate the Equal Protection Clause and Title VI; Grutter's permissive framework is effectively overruled. Race may be considered only as it relates to an applicant's individual experiences, never as a numerical 'plus' or category.

canonical_cases.case_name: Parents Involved in Community Schools v. Seattle School District No. 1
canonical_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
canonical_cases.holding: K-12 race-based assignment plans intended to maintain racial balance fail strict scrutiny; achieving diversity for its own sake is not a compelling interest in K-12, and individualized consideration is required.

canonical_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
canonical_cases.holding: Historical context (effectively overruled by SFFA): held that universities could consider race as one factor in admissions to achieve the educational benefits of diversity.

canonical_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
canonical_cases.holding: Race-based classifications by any level of government (federal or state) are subject to strict scrutiny; the same standard applies regardless of the racial group benefited or burdened.

canonical_statutes.citation: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Equal Protection Clause)
canonical_statutes.title: Fourteenth Amendment - Equal Protection (race classifications)
canonical_statutes.text: No State shall ... deny to any person within its jurisdiction the equal protection of the laws. Race-based classifications by government are presumptively unconstitutional and survive only if narrowly tailored to a compelling governmental interest.

doctrines.doctrine_name: Fourth Amendment in digital surveillance - Carpenter / Smith / Riley
doctrines.description: Carpenter v. United States held that long-term cell-site location records require a warrant; subsequent geofence-warrant cases (US v. Smith 5th Cir.; US v. Chatrie 4th Cir., 2024) divide on third-party-doctrine reach in the digital era.

canonical_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
canonical_cases.holding: The government's acquisition of seven days of historical cell-site location information (CSLI) constitutes a search under the Fourth Amendment and generally requires a warrant supported by probable cause. The third-party doctrine does not extend to the comprehensive chronicle of a person's movements revealed by CSLI.

canonical_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
canonical_cases.holding: Police generally may not, without a warrant, search digital information on a cell phone seized incident to arrest; the digital privacy stakes are too high to treat phones like cigarette packs.

canonical_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
canonical_cases.holding: Historical context: established the third-party doctrine - there is no reasonable expectation of privacy in numbers dialed and conveyed to the phone company. Carpenter limits but does not overrule Smith.

canonical_cases.court: Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
canonical_cases.holding: Held that a Google geofence warrant for a 30-minute window in a bank-robbery investigation did not violate the Fourth Amendment because the defendant lacked a reasonable expectation of privacy in the Google Location History data revealed.

canonical_cases.court: Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
canonical_cases.holding: The Fifth Circuit reached the opposite conclusion from the Fourth Circuit in Chatrie: a geofence warrant directed at Google's Location History database is a general search that lacks particularity and probable cause, violating the Fourth Amendment. Defendants had a reasonable expectation of privacy in their LH data.

canonical_statutes.title: Fourth Amendment
canonical_statutes.text: The right of the people to be secure in their persons, houses, papers, and effects, against unreasonable searches and seizures, shall not be violated, and no Warrants shall issue, but upon probable cause, supported by Oath or affirmation, and particularly describing the place to be searched, and the persons or things to be seized.

canonical_statutes.title: Stored Communications Act - disclosure of CSLI
canonical_statutes.text: A court order for disclosure under subsection (b) or (c) may be issued by any court that is a court of competent jurisdiction and shall issue only if the governmental entity offers specific and articulable facts showing that there are reasonable grounds to believe that the contents of a wire or electronic communication, or the records or other information sought, are relevant and material to an ongoing criminal investigation.

doctrines.doctrine_name: Cancellation of removal under INA § 240A - Wilkinson v. Garland
doctrines.description: Nonpermanent residents may obtain cancellation of removal under INA § 240A(b)(1) by showing 10 years' physical presence, good moral character, no disqualifying convictions, and 'exceptional and extremely unusual hardship' to a qualifying U.S. citizen or LPR relative. Wilkinson v. Garland (2024) makes the BIA's hardship determination judicially reviewable.

canonical_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
canonical_cases.holding: The 'exceptional and extremely unusual hardship' determination under INA § 240A(b)(1)(D) is a mixed question of law and fact, and federal courts have jurisdiction to review it under 8 U.S.C. § 1252(a)(2)(D); Patel v. Garland's bar on review extends only to predicate facts, not the application of the hardship standard.

canonical_cases.court: Board of Immigration Appeals
canonical_cases.holding: Established the 'exceptional and extremely unusual hardship' standard for cancellation: hardship must be substantially beyond the ordinary hardship that would result from a qualifying relative's removal.

canonical_cases.court: Board of Immigration Appeals
canonical_cases.holding: Refined the hardship standard, recognizing that a single mother with multiple U.S.-citizen children and no realistic ability to relocate them to Mexico had shown exceptional and extremely unusual hardship.

canonical_statutes.title: Cancellation of removal - nonpermanent residents
canonical_statutes.text: The Attorney General may cancel removal of, and adjust to the status of an alien lawfully admitted for permanent residence, an alien who is inadmissible or deportable from the United States if the alien - (A) has been physically present in the United States for a continuous period of not less than 10 years immediately preceding the date of such application; (B) has been a person of good moral character during such period; (C) has not been convicted of an offense under section 1182(a)(2), 1227(a)(2), or 1227(a)(3) of this title; and (D) establishes that removal would result in exceptional and extremely unusual hardship to the alien's spouse, parent, or child, who is a citizen of the United States or an alien lawfully admitted for permanent residence.

doctrines.doctrine_name: Waiver of fiduciary duties in Delaware LLCs (6 Del. C. § 18-1101)
doctrines.description: Delaware permits LLC operating agreements to expand, restrict, or eliminate fiduciary duties, provided the implied contractual covenant of good faith and fair dealing is preserved (§ 18-1101(c)). The implied covenant itself may not be waived.

canonical_cases.case_name: Manti Holdings, LLC v. Authentix Acquisition Co.
canonical_cases.court: Supreme Court of Delaware
canonical_cases.holding: Sophisticated parties to a Delaware LLC agreement may by clear contractual language waive even statutory appraisal rights; freedom of contract is a paramount principle under the DLLC Act, but waivers must be clear and unambiguous.

canonical_cases.case_name: Wood v. U.S. Bank National Ass'n
canonical_cases.court: Court of Chancery of Delaware
canonical_cases.holding: Confirmed that under § 18-1101(c), LLC agreements may eliminate fiduciary duties so long as the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing remains; Court of Chancery enforces explicit waivers consistent with statute.

canonical_cases.case_name: Miller v. HCP Trumpet Investments, LLC
canonical_cases.court: Supreme Court of Delaware
canonical_cases.holding: Implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing cannot be waived in an LLC agreement; it operates as a gap-filler when the contract is silent, and parties may not contract around it.

canonical_statutes.title: DLLC Act - fiduciary duties may be expanded or restricted
canonical_statutes.text: To the extent that, at law or in equity, a member or manager or other person has duties (including fiduciary duties) to a limited liability company or to another member or manager or to another person that is a party to or is otherwise bound by a limited liability company agreement, the member's or manager's or other person's duties may be expanded or restricted or eliminated by provisions in the limited liability company agreement; provided, that the limited liability company agreement may not eliminate the implied contractual covenant of good faith and fair dealing.

doctrines.doctrine_name: Chapter 11 plan releases - 11 U.S.C. § 1123(b)(6) + Harrington v. Purdue
doctrines.description: Chapter 11 plans may include 'any other appropriate provision not inconsistent with the applicable provisions of this title' under § 1123(b)(6), but Harrington v. Purdue (2024) confirms this catchall cannot authorize non-consensual third-party (non-debtor) releases.

canonical_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
canonical_cases.holding: The Bankruptcy Code does not authorize non-consensual releases of third-party claims against non-debtors as part of a Chapter 11 plan; § 1123(b)(6)'s catchall does not stretch that far.

canonical_cases.case_name: In re Metromedia Fiber Network, Inc.
canonical_cases.court: Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit
canonical_cases.holding: Pre-Harrington Second Circuit framework for non-debtor releases: permitted only in 'rare cases' supported by specific factors. Harrington largely supersedes this for non-consensual releases.

canonical_cases.court: Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit
canonical_cases.holding: Pre-Harrington Third Circuit position: rejected non-consensual third-party releases absent extraordinary circumstances. Harrington adopts a near-categorical bar in line with this view.

canonical_statutes.title: Catchall - contents of a Chapter 11 plan
canonical_statutes.text: Subject to subsection (a) of this section, a plan may - (6) include any other appropriate provision not inconsistent with the applicable provisions of this title.

canonical_statutes.title: Bankruptcy discharge - effect on non-debtors
canonical_statutes.text: Except as provided in subsection (a)(3) of this section, discharge of a debt of the debtor does not affect the liability of any other entity on, or the property of any other entity for, such debt.

doctrines.doctrine_name: State-law execution of wills (Florida v. New York)
doctrines.description: State will-execution formalities vary: Florida (Fla. Stat. § 732.502) requires two witnesses present at signing; New York (N.Y. EPTL § 3-2.1) similarly requires two witnesses, but with different attestation mechanics; New York also recognizes very narrow holographic-will exceptions under § 3-2.2.

canonical_cases.court: District Court of Appeal of Florida, Fourth District
canonical_cases.holding: Florida strictly enforces § 732.502 will-formality requirements; substantial compliance is insufficient if the statutory witness-presence requirement is not satisfied.

canonical_statutes.title: Florida - execution of wills
canonical_statutes.text: Every will must be in writing and executed as follows: (1) Testator's signature.-(a) The testator must sign the will at the end; or the testator's name must be subscribed at the end of the will by some other person in the testator's presence and by the testator's direction. (b) The signing must be: 1. In the presence of at least two attesting witnesses. (2) Witnesses.-Any witness must sign the will in the presence of the testator and in the presence of each other.

canonical_statutes.title: New York - execution and attestation of wills
canonical_statutes.text: Except for nuncupative and holographic wills authorized by 3-2.2, every will must be in writing, and executed and attested in the following manner: (1) The will must be signed at the end by the testator or, in the name of the testator, by another person in his presence and by his direction. (2) The signature of the testator shall be affixed to the will in the presence of each of the attesting witnesses, or shall be acknowledged by the testator to each of them. There shall be at least two attesting witnesses, who shall, within one 30 day period, both attest the testator's signature and sign their names and addresses at the end of the will.

canonical_statutes.title: New York - nuncupative and holographic wills
canonical_statutes.text: (a) For the purposes of this section, (1) A nuncupative will is one which is unwritten, and the making thereof by the testator and its provisions are clearly established by at least two witnesses. (2) A holographic will is one which is written entirely in the handwriting of the testator, and is not executed and attested in accordance with the formalities prescribed by 3-2.1. (b) A nuncupative or holographic will is valid only if made by: (1) A member of the armed forces of the United States while in actual military or naval service during a war or other armed conflict.

doctrines.description: The business judgment rule: a rebuttable presumption that Delaware corporate directors, in making a business decision, acted on an informed basis, in good faith, and in the honest belief the action was in the corporation's best interest; rebutted by gross negligence, bad faith, or a disabling conflict of interest.

canonical_cases.court: Supreme Court of Delaware
canonical_cases.holding: The business judgment rule is a presumption that in making a business decision the directors of a corporation acted on an informed basis, in good faith, and in the honest belief that the action taken was in the best interests of the company. Absent an abuse of discretion, that judgment will be respected by the courts.

canonical_cases.court: Supreme Court of Delaware
canonical_cases.holding: To invoke the business judgment rule's protection directors must inform themselves, prior to making a business decision, of all material information reasonably available to them; the presumption is rebutted by gross negligence, including a failure to be adequately informed.

doctrines.description: The constitutional fault standard for defamation of public officials and public figures: knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard for the truth (actual malice).

canonical_cases.case_name: New York Times Co. v. Sullivan
canonical_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
canonical_cases.holding: A public official may not recover for a defamatory falsehood relating to official conduct unless he proves the statement was made with 'actual malice' - with knowledge that it was false or with reckless disregard of whether it was false or not.

canonical_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
canonical_cases.holding: A private figure need only show fault (at least negligence), not actual malice, to recover actual damages for defamation; states may not impose liability without fault.

doctrines.doctrine_name: Sixth Amendment right to appointed counsel
doctrines.description: The Sixth Amendment right to counsel is fundamental and obligatory on the states; indigent defendants charged with serious crimes are entitled to appointed counsel.

canonical_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
canonical_cases.holding: The Sixth Amendment's guarantee of counsel is a fundamental right made obligatory on the states by the Fourteenth Amendment; a state must provide counsel to an indigent defendant charged with a serious offense who cannot afford a lawyer.

doctrines.description: The power of the federal courts to review acts of Congress and the executive and to declare void those repugnant to the Constitution.

canonical_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
canonical_cases.holding: It is emphatically the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is; a legislative act repugnant to the Constitution is void, and courts must not give it effect. This established judicial review.

doctrines.description: The doctrine by which most Bill of Rights guarantees are applied to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause.

canonical_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
canonical_cases.holding: The Second Amendment right to keep and bear arms recognized in Heller is fully applicable to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause; most Bill of Rights guarantees are selectively incorporated against the states.

doctrines.doctrine_name: Eighth Amendment limit on felony-murder death penalty
doctrines.description: Eighth Amendment limits on capital punishment for a felony-murder participant who did not kill, attempt to kill, or intend a killing.

canonical_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
canonical_cases.holding: The Eighth Amendment forbids the death penalty for a defendant who aids and abets a felony in which a murder is committed by others but who does not himself kill, attempt to kill, or intend that a killing take place or that lethal force be used.

canonical_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
canonical_cases.holding: The death penalty may be imposed on a felony-murder participant who was a major participant in the underlying felony and acted with reckless indifference to human life, even absent an intent to kill.

doctrines.description: The First Amendment standard for punishing advocacy of force or law violation: directed to inciting imminent lawless action and likely to produce it.

canonical_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
canonical_cases.holding: The government may not forbid advocacy of the use of force or of law violation except where such advocacy is directed to inciting or producing imminent lawless action and is likely to incite or produce such action.

doctrines.doctrine_name: Probable cause - totality of the circumstances
doctrines.description: The totality-of-the-circumstances test for probable cause supporting warrants and warrantless arrests.

canonical_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
canonical_cases.holding: Probable cause is assessed under a practical, common-sense totality-of-the-circumstances test, replacing the rigid two-pronged Aguilar-Spinelli test for evaluating an informant's tip.

doctrines.doctrine_name: Consideration - forbearance of a legal right
doctrines.description: Forbearance from exercising a legal right, at the promisor's request, is valid consideration even without economic benefit to the promisor.

canonical_cases.court: Court of Appeals of New York
canonical_cases.holding: Forbearance - a nephew giving up drinking, smoking, swearing, and gambling at his uncle's request - is valid consideration; the promisee's abandonment of a legal right is sufficient to support the promise even though the promisor received no economic benefit.

doctrines.description: A residential lease carries an implied warranty of habitability, measured by the housing code, on which the tenant's duty to pay rent depends.

canonical_cases.case_name: Javins v. First National Realty Corp.
canonical_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit
canonical_cases.holding: A warranty of habitability, measured by the standards of the housing code, is implied by operation of law into residential leases; the tenant's obligation to pay rent is dependent on the landlord's performance of that warranty, so breach may be raised as a defense to eviction for nonpayment.

doctrines.doctrine_name: Burden of proof for affirmative defenses
doctrines.description: A state may constitutionally require a defendant to prove an affirmative defense so long as the prosecution still proves every element of the offense beyond a reasonable doubt.

canonical_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
canonical_cases.holding: A state may place on the defendant the burden of proving an affirmative defense (there, extreme emotional disturbance) by a preponderance of the evidence without violating due process, so long as it does not shift or relieve the prosecution's burden to prove each element of the crime beyond a reasonable doubt.

doctrines.description: The scope of the corporate attorney-client privilege; rejection of the narrow control-group test.

canonical_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
canonical_cases.holding: The corporate attorney-client privilege is not limited to a 'control group' of senior management; it protects communications between counsel and employees at any level made, at the direction of superiors, to secure legal advice for the corporation.

doctrines.doctrine_name: Negligence per se (statutory standard of care)
doctrines.description: An unexcused violation of a statute enacted to protect a class of persons from a type of harm is negligence in itself.

canonical_cases.court: Court of Appeals of New York
canonical_cases.holding: The unexcused omission of a statutory duty (there, driving without lights) is negligence in itself; jurors are not free to treat the disregard of a safety statute enacted for the protection of others as immaterial.
